ruling_gist_en: According to the provisions of Article 79, Item (3) of the Maritime Law of the People's Republic of China, an order bill of lading not bearing the name of the consignee may be transferred by blank endorsement. However, after the holder of the bill of lading has exchanged one set of the original bills of lading for a delivery order, it is no longer possible for the parties to transfer the full set of original bills of lading. Therefore, any subsequent purported transfer of the bills of lading shall have no binding effect on the parties.

full_text_en:
Concordia Agricultural Products Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. v. Guangdong Fuhong Oil Products Co., Ltd., and Third Party: China Construction Bank Corporation, Zhanjiang Branch — Dispute over Confirmation of Ownership

【Ruling Summary】

Pursuant to the provisions of Article 79(3) of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China, a blank endorsed order bill of lading may be transferred by blank endorsement. However, when the holder of the bill of lading has exchanged one set of original bills of lading for a delivery order, it becomes impossible for the party to transfer the entire set of original bills of lading. Consequently, any subsequent so-called transfer of the bill of lading is not binding on the parties.

Article 23 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China provides that the creation and transfer of real rights in movables shall take effect upon delivery. Whether delivery is completed is the standard for determining whether ownership of movables has been transferred. Where movables are in the possession of a third party, constructive delivery shall be effected in accordance with Article 26 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China. Article 88 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Security Law of the People's Republic of China stipulates that where a pledgor pledges property in indirect possession, the pledge shall be deemed to have been delivered upon written notice to the possessor of the pledge contract. In line with the spirit of this provision, delivery of a delivery order merely signifies the transfer of the party's right to demand delivery. Where the party has not notified the actual possessor of the transfer of the right to demand delivery, the delivery of the delivery order does not constitute constructive delivery under Article 26 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2010) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 20

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): Concordia Agricultural Products Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. Domicile: Building 1, No. 110-120 Guangling Fourth Road, Hongkou District, Shanghai.

Legal Representative: Cai Li, President of the Company's China Region.

Agent ad litem: Huang Zhuo, Lawyer of Guangdong Zhengda Lianhe Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Yang Meihua, Lawyer of Guangdong Zhengda Lianhe Law Firm.

Appellee (Defendant at First Instance): Guangdong Fuhong Oil Products Co., Ltd. Domicile: No. 5 Huguang Road, Xiashan District, Zhanjiang, Guangdong Province.

Legal Representative: Luo Jun, General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Wang Zhen, Lawyer of Liaoning Wenzheng Law Firm.

Third Party at First Instance: China Construction Bank Corporation, Zhanjiang Branch. Domicile: No. 46, Renmin Avenue Middle, Zhanjiang, Guangdong Province.

Person in Charge: Chen Zenghua, President of the Branch.

Agent ad litem: Xue Feng, Lawyer of Beijing Kaiyu Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Baohua, Lawyer of Tianyang (Beijing) Law Firm.

The appellant, Concordia Agricultural Products Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Concordia), appealed to this Court against the civil judgment (2009) Hu Gao Min Er (Shang) Chu Zi No. 4 rendered by the Shanghai High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance) in the case of a dispute over confirmation of ownership with the appellee, Guangdong Fuhong Oil Products Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Fuhong), and the third party at first instance, China Construction Bank Corporation, Zhanjiang Branch (hereinafter referred to as Zhanjiang CCB). This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law, with Judge Chen Jizhong as the presiding judge, and Acting Judges Gao Xiaoli and Shen Hongyu participating in the deliberation. The case was heard in open court on September 27, 2010, with Court Clerk Zhang Bona serving as the recorder. The agents ad litem of the appellant Concordia, Huang Zhuo and Yang Meihua, the agent ad litem of the appellee Fuhong, Wang Zhen, and the agents ad litem of the third party at first instance Zhanjiang CCB, Xue Feng and Zhang Baohua, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. This case is now concluded.

Concordia filed a complaint with the court of first instance, alleging: In June 2008, Concordia transferred 10,186.03 tons of Argentine soybeans shipped on the vessel "Maca" to Fuhong at an agreed unit price of RMB 4,075 per ton (unless otherwise specified, all currency amounts are in RMB). On September 10 of the same year, Fuhong pledged the Argentine soybeans shipped on the vessel "Kangjin" and the corresponding bills of lading to Concordia. On September 15 and October 8, the two parties signed a "Confirmation Letter" and a "Goods Swap Agreement," stipulating that Concordia would swap 52,231 tons of Argentine soybeans shipped on the "Maca" with an equal quantity of Argentine soybeans shipped on the "Kangjin" owned by Fuhong. Fuhong had already taken delivery of the soybeans on the "Maca" used for the swap. During the performance of the loan contract between Fuhong and Zhanjiang CCB, Fuhong failed to truthfully disclose the ownership of the soybeans on the "Kangjin," leading Zhanjiang CCB to believe that the 52,231 tons of soybeans stored in Zhanjiang Port belonged to Fuhong. On November 28, 2008, Zhanjiang CCB applied to the Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Zhanjiang Intermediate Court) for a freeze on the soybeans. Concordia filed an objection to the preservation measure with the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court but was informed that "the ownership of the frozen soybeans must be determined through substantive trial," and the freeze was not lifted. Concordia therefore filed this lawsuit, requesting a judgment that Fuhong cease infringing on Concordia's ownership of the 52,231 tons of Argentine soybeans (valued at RMB 212,841,325) shipped on the "Kangjin" and stored at Zhanjiang Port terminal, and remove the obstruction. On April 28, 2009, upon the application of Zhanjiang CCB, the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court sold the disputed soybeans and placed the proceeds in escrow. Accordingly, Concordia amended its claims to: 1. Confirmation that the ownership of the 52,231 tons of Argentine soybeans originally stored at Zhanjiang Port terminal, which were shipped on the "Kangjin" and subsequently frozen and sold, belongs to Concordia; 2. Judgment that the proceeds from the sale of the 52,231 tons of Argentine soybeans shipped on the "Kangjin" held in escrow by the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court, along with the corresponding interest, belong to Concordia and shall be collected by Concordia.

The court of first instance found the following facts: On April 18, 2008, Concordia and Fuhong entered into an "Agent Import Agreement," under which Concordia was to act as the import agent for Fuhong for Argentine soybeans. After the 64,000 tons of soybeans shipped on the "Maca" arrived at port, Fuhong exchanged the original bills of lading for the "Maca" for a delivery order. On July 24, 2008, Fuhong applied to Zhanjiang CCB for the issuance of a usance letter of credit for the import of the goods on the "Kangjin," and on the same day issued a "Trust Receipt" to Zhanjiang CCB, confirming: "This company agrees and acknowledges that your bank holds or, from the date of issuance of this trust receipt, acquires ownership of the above documents and the goods they represent. At the same time, this trust receipt establishes a trust legal relationship between your bank and this company. Your bank is the trustor and beneficiary, this company is the trustee, and the above documents and the goods they represent are the trust property." On July 25, 2008, Zhanjiang CCB signed a "Notice of Utilization of Trade Finance Facility," agreeing to allow Fuhong to utilize a trade finance facility of USD 23.8 million for the issuance of a letter of credit (L/C No. 44710010001034), and issued a "Notice of Issuance of Letter of Credit" to Fuhong.

Before September 9, 2008, Fuhong obtained the full set of original bills of lading for the goods on the "Kangjin" from Zhanjiang CCB and entrusted Zhanjiang Yuexi Import & Export Freight Agency Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yuexi Freight) with customs declaration. On September 10, 2008, Concordia and Fuhong entered into a "Pledge Contract," stipulating that Fuhong would pledge to Concordia the full set of marine bills of lading for the "Kangjin" and the 52,231 tons of goods thereunder. Concordia confirmed receipt of the full set of marine bills of lading from Fuhong, and Fuhong undertook to either replace the goods with physical goods or pay Concordia in full within two months. On September 15, 2008, Concordia and Fuhong signed a "Confirmation Letter," confirming that, by way of "new goods" replacing "old goods," Fuhong would repay Concordia for the soybeans it had taken delivery of but not yet paid for; Fuhong confirmed the transfer of ownership of the 52,231 tons of soybeans on the "Kangjin" to Concordia, and Concordia confirmed the transfer of ownership of its 52,231 tons of soybeans to Fuhong; upon the transfer of ownership of the 52,231 tons of soybeans on the "Kangjin" to Concordia, the aforementioned Pledge Contract would automatically lapse. On September 16, 2008, the "Kangjin" arrived at Zhanjiang Port. On September 18, 2008, Fuhong exchanged the original marine bills of lading with the shipowner of the "Kangjin" for a set of delivery orders (five copies) for the 52,231 tons of soybeans on the "Kangjin." The delivery order bore the official seals of Fuhong and Zhanjiang Yuanheng Shipping Agency Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yuanheng). On October 8, 2008, Concordia and Fuhong signed a "Goods Swap Agreement," stating that, due to Fuhong's failure to take delivery of the goods on the "Maca" as agreed, which could affect the quality of the goods, Concordia and Fuhong agreed to swap the goods on the "Maca," "Aihua," and "Kangjin" as follows: Fuhong had already swapped its 35,000 tons of soybeans on the "Aihua" for an equal quantity of 35,000 tons of unpaid soybeans on the "Maca" that had been imported by Concordia on behalf of Fuhong and that Fuhong had taken delivery of in advance; Fuhong now swapped its 52,231 tons of soybeans on the "Kangjin" in exchange for the 35,000 tons of soybeans on the "Aihua" used in the first swap and the remaining 17,231 tons of soybeans on the "Maca," i.e., the ownership of the 52,231 tons of soybeans on the "Kangjin" belonged to Concordia, and the ownership of the 17,231 tons of soybeans on the "Maca" and the 35,000 tons of soybeans on the "Aihua" belonged to Fuhong. On the same day, Fuhong issued a power of attorney to Yuanheng, informing Yuanheng that, in accordance with the Goods Swap Agreement, it had transferred the ownership of the 52,231 tons of soybeans on the "Kangjin" to Concordia, and now fully authorized Yuanheng to handle the delivery and taking delivery of the above goods.

On December 10, 2008, Concordia and Fuhong reconciled the accounts regarding the outstanding amounts. On December 16, 2008, Concordia and Fuhong signed a "Supplementary Agreement" in Shanghai, stipulating that any disputes arising from the Confirmation Letter and the Goods Swap Agreement, if not resolved through negotiation, could be brought by either party to a competent court at the place of contract signing. On April 7, 2009, Concordia filed this lawsuit with the court of first instance.

It was further found that, because Fuhong failed to accept and pay the negotiating bank abroad by the negotiation date, Zhanjiang CCB, after deducting the margin of RMB 23.52 million, on December 3, 2008, paid USD 29,322,013.95 on behalf of Fuhong to the negotiating bank abroad as a payment under the letter of credit. As of July 31, 2009, Fuhong had repaid interest of USD 141,515.37 on this advance payment, but the principal remained unpaid. After fruitless demands for payment, Zhanjiang CCB filed a lawsuit against Fuhong and Fuhong Group Co., Ltd. with the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court ([2009] Zhan Zhong Fa Min San Chu Zi No. 3). On November 28, 2008, upon the application of Zhanjiang CCB for pre-litigation property preservation, the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court issued a civil ruling ([2008] Zhan Zhong Fa Bao Zi No. 29) and, on November 30, 2008, placed a sequential freeze on approximately 72,000 tons of soybeans discharged from the "Aihua" and "Kangjin" and stored in the warehouse of Zhanjiang Port (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhanjiang Port Company) (the freeze in case [2009] Zhan Zhong Fa Min San Chu Zi No. 1, accepted by the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court, was the first-priority freeze on that batch of soybeans). On December 4, 2008, Concordia, holding the delivery order, went to Zhanjiang Port Company to request delivery. Zhanjiang Port Company replied in writing: "If the consignee on the delivery order, as shown by the seal, is inconsistent with the owner of the goods presenting the delivery order, the owner presenting the delivery order must provide relevant documents showing that the sealed consignee has consented to the transfer of ownership of the goods to such owner. Now that your company has submitted to our company the delivery order and the documents regarding the transfer of ownership of the above goods to request delivery, because the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court has already frozen the goods, we cannot handle the related delivery procedures. After our company confirms that the court has lifted the freeze, if your company submits to our company the original of the aforementioned delivery order and the documents regarding the transfer of ownership, our company agrees to release to your company the goods under the aforementioned delivery order that have been legally cleared through customs." On November 28, 2008, Concordia, on the ground that the frozen 52,231 tons of soybeans on the "Kangjin" belonged to it, raised an objection to the preservation measure and requested the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court to lift the freeze. On December 11, 2008, upon the application of Zhanjiang CCB, the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court ruled to lift the freeze on approximately 17,600 tons of soybeans on the "Aihua." On January 7, 2009, after the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court ruled to permit the plaintiff in the aforementioned case [2009] Zhan Zhong Fa Min San Chu Zi No. 1, the Agricultural Development Bank of China Zhanjiang Branch, to withdraw its lawsuit, the freeze in the present case was converted to a formal freeze. On March 17, 2009, the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court notified Concordia in writing that its objection to the ownership of the 52,231 tons of soybeans on the "Kangjin" could only be determined through substantive trial, and thus the freeze would not be lifted. Considering that long-term storage would affect the quality of the soybeans, on March 23, 2009, the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court ruled to sell the batch of soybeans. After actual transfer and counting, 51,854.92 tons of soybeans were sold at a unit price of RMB 2,640 per ton, yielding proceeds of RMB 136,896,988.80 (excluding customs duties, value-added tax and late payment surcharges, port charges, etc., which remain payable), which were deposited into the account of the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court. On April 1, 2008, the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court notified Concordia to participate in the case as a third party without independent claims. On August 28, 2009, the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court rendered a civil judgment ([2009] Zhan Zhong Fa Min San Chu Zi No. 3). None of the parties appealed, and the civil judgment has become final.

The court of first instance held that the issues in dispute primarily focused on the following three aspects: First, whether this case and the letter of credit financing dispute case in the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court constitute two lawsuits on the same matter; second, the legal nature and validity of the trust receipt; third, whether Concordia had obtained ownership of the disputed goods on the "Kangjin."

I. Whether this case and the letter of credit financing dispute case in the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court constitute two lawsuits on the same matter

Zhanjiang CCB argued that the ownership of the disputed goods on the "Kangjin" had already been adjudicated by the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court in the letter of credit financing dispute case, and therefore Concordia's lawsuit constituted a duplicate action. Concordia argued that, as a third party without independent claims in the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court letter of credit financing dispute case, it was not precluded from filing this lawsuit before the court of first instance. Fuhong agreed with Concordia's position.

The court of first instance held that the principle of "res judicata" under China's Civil Procedure Law means that the same parties may not file a new lawsuit based on the same facts and the same subject matter of the action. The subject matter of an action refers to the civil legal relationship or substantive right in dispute. In this case: First, the basis of the claims in this case and the letter of credit financing dispute case in the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court are different. This case is based on the barter contract legal relationship between Concordia and Fuhong, while the letter of credit financing dispute case in the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court is based on the letter of credit legal relationship and the trust receipt legal relationship between Zhanjiang CCB and Fuhong. The subject matters of the two actions are not identical. Second, as a third party without independent claims in the letter of credit financing dispute case in the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court, Concordia was unable to raise independent claims. If it were not allowed to raise independent claims in this case, it would effectively deprive it of its right to sue as an interested party in the ownership dispute. Third, although the letter of credit financing dispute case in the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court has been finally judged in the first instance, the determination of the ownership of the disputed goods on the "Kangjin" in that judgment constitutes an established fact. Pursuant to Article 9 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, the parties are not required to prove such facts again. However, if Concordia has sufficient evidence to rebut them, the court of first instance may still make a determination inconsistent with the aforementioned established fact. Moreover, Fuhong admitted all the facts alleged by Zhanjiang CCB in the letter of credit financing dispute case in the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court, but in this case, it claimed that the ownership of the disputed goods on the "Kangjin" had been transferred to Concordia. Fuhong's statements in the two cases are contradictory. Therefore, Concordia's filing of this lawsuit complies with the conditions for filing a lawsuit under the Civil Procedure Law and does not violate the principle of "res judicata."

II. The legal nature and validity of the trust receipt

Zhanjiang CCB argued that the trust receipt is evidence of the trust contract relationship between it and Fuhong and also evidence of its ownership of the trust property. Therefore, the ownership of the disputed goods on the "Kangjin" in this case should belong to it. Concordia argued that the trust receipt is not a real right document and that the third party does not have ownership of the disputed goods on the "Kangjin." Fuhong argued that the ownership of the disputed goods on the "Kangjin" had been transferred to Concordia.

The court of first instance held that, as a type of agreement commonly used in international trade, the main function of a trust receipt is to provide financing convenience for the applicant (the importer) while protecting the bank's claims. Under China's current legal framework: On the one hand, a trust receipt does not establish a trust legal relationship between the issuing bank and the applicant. The reason is that, according to the provisions of the Trust Law of China, trust property must be property or property rights lawfully owned by the trustor. Therefore, the issuing bank's property right in the documents under the letter of credit is a prerequisite for the validity of a trust legal relationship. However, the agreement in this trust receipt is contrary to the basic logic of the aforementioned legal provisions, making it difficult to apply the relevant provisions of the Trust Law. On the other hand, a trust receipt does not indicate the establishment of a pledge legal relationship between the issuing bank and the applicant. Because the Security Law of China requires the transfer of possession as a condition for the validity of a pledge of movables. In this case, after obtaining the full set of marine bills of lading, the issuing bank immediately handed them over to the applicant. The issuing bank did not actually possess the documents under the letter of credit or the imported goods. Therefore, no valid pledge legal relationship existed between the issuing bank and the applicant. Accordingly, under current legal provisions, a trust receipt can be regarded as an innominate contract between the importer and the issuing bank. The issuing bank, based on the agreement in the trust receipt with the importer, has a priority right to compensation over the imported goods under the letter of credit. However, because the trust receipt lacks publicity, it is binding only on the importer and the issuing bank, and neither party can use the trust receipt to oppose a bona fide third party.

III. Whether Concordia had obtained ownership of the disputed goods on the "Kangjin"

According to the relevant provisions of the Contract Law and the Property Law of China, ownership of movables is transferred upon delivery of the subject matter, unless otherwise provided by law or agreed by the parties. In this case, Concordia and Zhanjiang CCB dispute the ownership of the disputed goods on the "Kangjin."

The court of first instance held: First, after the disputed goods on the "Kangjin" entered the warehouse, they were lawfully frozen by the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court. When Concordia, holding the relevant documents, requested delivery, Zhanjiang Port Company informed it that it could go through the delivery procedures by presenting the delivery order and the original documents of the ownership transfer only after the court lifted the freeze. Subsequently, the disputed goods on the "Kangjin" were ordered to be sold by the Zhanjiang Intermediate Court. It can be seen that Concordia never actually possessed the disputed goods on the "Kangjin."

Secondly, an original ocean bill of lading is a document of title. The holder possesses the right to take delivery of the goods under the bill of lading. However, a delivery order obtained by exchanging the original ocean bill of lading with the carrier does not have the nature of a document of title. It merely proves that the cargo owner or the delivery unit recorded on the delivery order has the right to take delivery of the goods and is essentially a document of claim. In this case, Kenko Dia Company claimed that both Fuhong Company and Yuanheng Company were entrusted by it to exchange the original ocean bill of lading for the delivery order. However, the evidence it submitted was insufficient to prove this fact. Moreover, the delivery unit recorded on the delivery order held by Kenko Dia Company was Fuhong Company. Fuhong Company directly presented the original ocean bill of lading to the carrier of the Kangjin vessel without endorsing and transferring the bill of lading to another party, and obtained a delivery order recording Fuhong Company as the delivery unit. Therefore, the delivery of the goods under the Kangjin vessel to Kenko Dia Company, as claimed by Kenko Dia Company, was not completed.

In summary, this court holds that the goods under the Kangjin vessel were not delivered to Kenko Dia Company, and no other circumstances as provided by law existed, so the ownership of the goods did not change. Therefore, Kenko Dia Company's claims for confirmation that the goods under the Kangjin vessel and the proceeds from their sale belong to it, and for Fuhong Company to cease infringement and remove obstacles, lack factual and legal basis. This court does not support them in accordance with the law. As for the losses suffered by Kenko Dia Company due to its failure to obtain ownership of the goods under the Kangjin vessel, this constitutes a creditor-debtor relationship between it and Fuhong Company. Kenko Dia Company may assert its claims against Fuhong Company separately based on the 《Goods Swap Agreement》.

Accordingly, pursuant to Article 133, Article 174, and Article 175 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 23 and Article 33 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows: Kenko Dia Company's claims are not supported. Court acceptance fee of RMB 1,106,007 shall be borne by Kenko Dia Company.

Kenko Dia Company, dissatisfied with the original judgment, appealed to this court, stating:

I. The original trial court's improper evaluation of evidence submitted by Kenko Dia Company and Fuhong Company seriously affected the determination of key facts in this case.
(1) The "Circumstances Explanation" issued by Yuanheng Company on June 27, 2009, submitted by Kenko Dia Company, proves that Yuanheng Company obtained the original bill of lading on behalf of Kenko Dia Company and completed the delivery of the goods. In this case, given the objective circumstances, Fuhong Company, as a party, acknowledged Kenko Dia Company's evidence, and the evidence provided by Fuhong Company corroborated this evidence; Zhanjiang Construction Bank did not submit any rebuttal evidence, only denying the authenticity of the evidence because it was unaware and unfavorable to it. The original trial court, on the grounds that "Zhanjiang Construction Bank did not confirm its authenticity, and Kenko Dia Company also failed to provide other evidence to corroborate it," refused to admit the above evidence and did not confirm the facts Kenko Dia Company claimed based on this evidence, which does not comply with legal provisions.
(2) Regarding the witness testimony of Yuan Weifeng provided by Fuhong Company. Yuan Weifeng is a shareholder of Fuhong Company. When Kenko Dia Company entrusted Fuhong Company and Yuanheng Company to handle the relevant procedures, Yuan Weifeng was the person in charge of this aspect of Fuhong Company's work. Fuhong Company also acknowledged that Yuan Weifeng's opinion represented the company's opinion; Yuan Weifeng's witness testimony corroborated the evidence submitted by Kenko Dia Company and was not isolated evidence, so it should be admitted. The original trial court's adverse judgment against Kenko Dia Company due to formal defects in Fuhong Company's evidence was clearly unfair to Kenko Dia Company.
(3) The original trial court should not have automatically accepted the judgment of Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court. In that case, Kenko Dia Company was a third party without independent claims. The Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court did not rule in the main text that Kenko Dia Company did not acquire ownership of the goods, but rather mentioned this issue in its reasoning. However, its reasoning was based on an erroneous premise: that a blank-endorsed bill of lading cannot be transferred. According to Article 79 of the Maritime Law, an order bill of lading may be transferred by special endorsement or blank endorsement. In this case, Fuhong Company's blank endorsement and transfer of the bill of lading to Kenko Dia Company was not improper, and the reasoning premise of the Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court was inconsistent with legal provisions. Therefore, the conclusion could not comply with legal provisions either.

II. The original trial court's findings of fact were erroneous and the application of law was improper.
(1) The original trial court's finding that Fuhong Company delivered the complete set of ocean bills of lading to Kenko Dia Company was erroneous. On September 5, 2008, Fuhong Company delivered the complete set of ocean bills of lading, endorsed in blank by Fuhong Company, to Kenko Dia Company's agent, Yuanheng Company. During the trial, Fuhong Company also acknowledged the delivery of the bills of lading, and the evidence it submitted and the explanation from Yuanheng Company corroborated each other regarding the above facts. After Fuhong Company delivered the bills of lading, the complete set of bills of lading and the delivery order obtained in exchange for them were held by Kenko Dia Company. The original trial court, without reasonable grounds, refused to admit the evidence of Kenko Dia Company and Fuhong Company, leading to erroneous findings of fact.
(2) The original trial court's understanding and application of the law regarding the blank-endorsed bill of lading in question were erroneous. According to Article 79 of the Maritime Law, a bill of lading endorsed in blank is a freely transferable bill of lading. In this case, Fuhong Company had already endorsed the bill of lading in blank and then transferred it to Kenko Dia Company. The original trial court's finding that Fuhong Company did not endorse and transfer the bill of lading to another party was an error in fact-finding and an error in the application of law.
(3) The original trial court's findings regarding the agency relationship between Fuhong Company and Yuanheng Company were erroneous, and the application of law was improper. In this case, because Fuhong Company was the notify party on the bill of lading and was a party to the barter contract obligated to assist in transferring ownership to Kenko Dia Company, Kenko Dia Company entrusted Fuhong Company and Yuanheng Company as its agents to handle the procedures for taking delivery of the goods. Pursuant to Articles 402 and 403 of the Contract Law, the agent has the right to engage in civil acts, including entering into contracts with third parties, in its own name within the scope of authority granted by the principal. The original trial court did not apply these legal provisions to determine the agency relationship between Fuhong Company and Yuanheng Company. During the period when Kenko Dia Company possessed the bill of lading, the legal consequences of Fuhong Company and Yuanheng Company's acts of exchanging the bill of lading on its behalf should be borne by the principal, Kenko Dia Company.
(4) The original trial court's findings regarding the entries on the delivery order were erroneous. In this case, after Fuhong Company obtained the order bill of lading, it endorsed it in blank and then delivered it to Kenko Dia Company. Therefore, when Fuhong Company and Yuanheng Company exchanged the bill of lading for the delivery order on behalf of Kenko Dia Company, the bill of lading received by the carrier was not a straight bill of lading but a blank-endorsed order bill of lading. Consequently, the delivery order obtained did not specify the consignee (the consignee was recorded as "To order"). In fact, the delivery order issued by Zhanjiang Ocean Shipping Agency (hereinafter referred to as Zhanjiang Ocean Shipping Agency) also did not specify the consignee (or delivery unit). Instead, to avoid unnecessary disputes, Kenko Dia Company requested Fuhong Company to affix its official seal in the "delivery unit" column. The reply letter from Zhanjiang Port Company also affirmed Kenko Dia Company's right to take delivery of the goods using the delivery order in question. The original trial court's finding that "a delivery order recording Fuhong Company as the delivery unit was obtained" was clearly inconsistent with the facts.
(5) The original trial court's factual findings regarding the transfer of ownership of the goods were erroneous, and the application of law was improper. On September 15, 2008, Kenko Dia Company and Fuhong Company had obtained ownership of each other's goods through barter. Fuhong Company delivered the bill of lading to Kenko Dia Company. Kenko Dia Company lawfully took possession of the goods by obtaining the bill of lading; on September 10, 2008, Fuhong Company had pledged the rights under the bill of lading and the goods of the "Kangjin" vessel to Kenko Dia Company, and Kenko Dia Company obtained priority right of compensation over the goods; on September 15, 2008, after the two parties confirmed the barter, ownership of the goods under the "Kangjin" vessel was transferred from Fuhong Company to Kenko Dia Company from the time of confirmation by both parties.

Requests: 1. Set aside the original judgment; 2. Confirm that ownership of the 52,231 tons of Argentine soybeans originally stored at Zhanjiang Port terminal under the "Kangjin" vessel, which were seized and sold, belongs to Kenko Dia Company; 3. Confirm that the sale proceeds of the 52,231 tons of Argentine soybeans under the "Kangjin" vessel deposited with the Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court and the corresponding interest belong to Kenko Dia Company; 4. The litigation costs of this case shall be borne by Fuhong Company and Zhanjiang Construction Bank.

Fuhong Company did not submit a written defense. At the second instance trial, Fuhong Company stated: 1. After the first instance judgment, the main leaders of Fuhong Company were detained and the company's accounts were sealed, so no appeal was filed. It has no objection to Kenko Dia Company's appeal; 2. Zhanjiang Construction Bank has fully recovered the loan amount and has suffered no loss; 3. From the signing of the goods import agency agreement between Fuhong Company and Kenko Dia Company on April 18, 2008, to Zhanjiang Construction Bank's issuance of the letter of credit and the signing of the pledge contract confirmation letter between Fuhong Company and Kenko Dia Company on September 4, 2008, these were all objective facts. Fuhong Company did not engage in malicious collusion with any party. As for the validity of these acts, it requests the People's Court to confirm in accordance with the law.

Zhanjiang Construction Bank did not submit a written statement. At the second instance trial, Zhanjiang Construction Bank stated: 1. The soybeans in question have been sold. According to the provisions of the Property Law, when the object no longer exists, the property right cannot exist, and currency adopts the rule of possession-is-ownership. Therefore, Kenko Dia Company's appeal claims cannot be sustained. 2. The investigation record of Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court proves that one original bill of lading was delivered by Fuhong Company to Yuanheng Company before September 9, 2008, so Fuhong Company did not transfer the complete set of original bills of lading to Kenko Dia Company. The confirmation letter and pledge contract were both signed after September 9, 2008. At that time, the bill of lading had already lost its effect as a document of title. The stipulations of the relevant facts contradict the objective facts, and their validity should not be confirmed. 3. All evidence proves that Fuhong Company is the cargo owner and that there is no agency relationship between it and Kenko Dia Company. It requests the appeal be dismissed and the original judgment affirmed.

This court holds: Based on Kenko Dia Company's claims at first instance, this case is essentially a dispute over confirmation of ownership, not a dispute over a sales contract. The cause of action determined in the original judgment was inappropriate and should be corrected.

This case does not involve foreign (including Hong Kong, Macau, or Taiwan) elements. The parties have no dispute regarding the application of law in this case, and this court confirms that.

During the second instance, none of the parties submitted new evidence to this court.

Based on Kenko Dia Company's appeal claims and the statements of Fuhong Company and Zhanjiang Construction Bank at the second instance trial, the parties confirmed that the issue in dispute in this case is: whether Kenko Dia Company owns the disputed soybeans.

According to Kenko Dia Company's statement at the second instance trial, it believes that the original judgment was erroneous in the factual finding that Fuhong Company obtained the delivery order using the original bill of lading on September 18, 2008, but that other facts were objective. Regarding this part of the facts, Kenko Dia Company claims that Fuhong Company delivered the bill of lading in question to it (with blank endorsement) on September 5, 2008, and thereafter, an agency relationship was formed between the two companies regarding the taking of delivery. To this end, Kenko Dia Company provided the witness testimony of Yuan Weifeng and the "Circumstances Explanation" issued by Yuanheng Company. Kenko Dia Company argues that these two pieces of evidence prove that the bill of lading in question had been endorsed and transferred to Kenko Dia Company, and that Fuhong Company acted on its behalf in exchanging the bill of lading for the delivery order.

Based on the facts confirmed by the effective civil judgment (No. [2009] Zhan Zhong Fa Min San Chu Zi No. 3) of Zhanjiang Intermediate People's Court and the content of the retention copy of the delivery order in question, the following facts can be established: Prior to September 9, 2008, Fuhong Company presented the original ocean bill of lading for the goods under the "Kangjin" vessel to Zhanjiang Ocean Shipping Agency, requesting to exchange it for a delivery order. On the same day, Fuhong Company received the customs declaration copy of the delivery order and on the same day entrusted Yuexi Cargo Agent to handle customs declaration. On September 18, 2008, Fuhong Company received a set (five copies) of the delivery order.

Kenko Dia Company's previous statements regarding when the bill of lading in question was delivered by Fuhong Company to it, as well as the content of the relevant evidence it submitted, are inconsistent: In the conversation record of the original trial court dated May 21, 2009, Kenko Dia Company stated that the bill of lading in question was delivered by Fuhong Company to it at the time the pledge contract was signed, and then it handed it over to the carrier with Fuhong Company's assistance; the "Circumstances Explanation" and Yuan Weifeng's witness testimony stated that the bill of lading was handed over to the carrier by Yuanheng Company and Fuhong Company together; at the trial of the original trial court on September 25, 2009, Kenko Dia Company then stated that Yuanheng Company collected the bill of lading on its behalf on September 5, 2008. This court holds that Kenko Dia Company's statements, as well as the "Circumstances Explanation" and Yuan Weifeng's witness testimony, are not credible. According to the established facts, although Fuhong Company only received the delivery order on September 18, 2008, Fuhong Company had already presented the bill of lading to Zhanjiang Ocean Shipping Agency and exchanged it for the customs declaration copy of the delivery order on September 9, 2008. The bill of lading in this case is a bearer order bill of lading. According to the relevant provisions of the Maritime Law, such a bill of lading can indeed be transferred by blank endorsement. However, the pledge contract, the confirmation letter, and the goods swap agreement were all signed after September 9, 2008. By that time, Fuhong Company could no longer have transferred the complete set of original bills of lading to Kenko Dia Company. Furthermore, Kenko Dia Company has no direct evidence to prove that it lawfully possessed the bill of lading on September 5, 2008. Therefore, Kenko Dia Company's claim that it received the bill of lading in question from Fuhong Company on September 5, 2008, lacks factual basis. This court does not support it.

Regarding whether an agency relationship existed between Kenko Dia Company and Fuhong Company. Currently, Kenko Dia Company has no direct evidence to prove the existence of an agency relationship between it and Fuhong Company. Furthermore, the "Circumstances Explanation" issued by Yuanheng Company and the witness testimony of Yuan Weifeng are inconsistent with the content of the delivery order recording Fuhong Company as the delivery unit. The above evidence is insufficient to prove the existence of an agency relationship. In fact, based on the facts of customs declaration and bill-of-lading exchange, the cargo owner of the soybeans in question was Fuhong Company, and it was Fuhong Company that directly exchanged the bill of lading for the delivery order with Zhanjiang Ocean Shipping Agency. Therefore, Kenko Dia Company's claim that an agency relationship existed between it and Fuhong Company lacks factual basis. This court does not support it.

Based on the foregoing analysis, the bill of lading in question was not transferred by Fuhong Company to Kenko Dia Company, but was held by Fuhong Company and exchanged for the delivery order. This is also corroborated by the fact that the delivery order records Fuhong Company as the delivery unit. Therefore, Kenko Dia Company's claim that it had lawfully taken possession of the goods in question by obtaining the bill of lading lacks factual basis. Pursuant to Article 23 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China, the creation and transfer of property rights in movables take effect upon delivery. Whether delivery is completed is the criterion for determining whether ownership of movables has been transferred. The goods in dispute in this case were stored at Zhanjiang Port, which is a situation of possession by a third party. In the absence of direct delivery in this case, only constructive delivery by direction can be used. Therefore, whether Fuhong Company completed constructive delivery by direction is the key to determining whether ownership of the disputed goods had been transferred. First, Kenko Dia Company and Fuhong Company have no evidence to prove when the delivery order was delivered. When Kenko Dia Company held the delivery order and requested to take delivery of the goods from Zhanjiang Port Company, the soybeans in question were already under seizure. Second, Article 88 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Guarantee Law of the People's Republic of China provides that if a pledgor pledges property held indirectly, delivery is deemed to have occurred when the pledge contract is notified in writing to the possessor. According to the spirit of this article, the delivery of the delivery order in this case only means that Fuhong Company's right to claim delivery of the goods was transferred to Kenko Dia Company. Where Fuhong Company has not notified the actual possessor of the transfer of the right to claim delivery, the delivery of the delivery order does not constitute constructive delivery by direction as stipulated in Article 26 of the Property Law of the People's Republic of China. Therefore, Fuhong Company did not complete the act of delivering the soybeans in question to Kenko Dia Company, and the ownership of the soybeans in question did not change. Kenko Dia Company's appellate claims that it is the owner of the soybeans in question and that the deposited funds for the soybeans in question belong to it lack factual and legal basis. This court does not support them.

In summary, Kenko Dia Company's appeal claims are without merit. This court does not support them. The original judgment found the facts basically clearly and applied the law correctly, and should be affirmed. Pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this court renders the following judgment:

Appeal dismissed; original judgment affirmed.

Court acceptance fee for the second instance of RMB 1,106,007 shall be borne by Kenko Dia Company.

This judgment is final.
